title: Case Study: Ride-Hailing (Uber)
summary: Design Uber end to end — matching a rider to the nearest driver, a trip that moves through states, and surge pricing that plugs in without touching the core.

blocks.markdown: **Design a ride-hailing service**: a rider requests a trip, the system matches the nearest available driver, the trip moves through a lifecycle from request to completion, a fare is estimated with surge pricing, and both sides rate each other afterward.

blocks.subTitle: Why this is an expert-level LLD problem
blocks.markdown:
Two things push this beyond a typical case study: **matching** is a live search over moving objects, not a static lookup, and the **trip** has more states than a simple on/off flag.

- The matching problem and the state-driven trip lifecycle are the two highlights of this design.
- Pricing and matching both change independently of the trip itself — a strong signal for **Strategy**. See [behavioral-patterns-i](behavioral-patterns-i).
- Use [lld-interview-framework](lld-interview-framework) as the general approach; this topic applies it to a harder, real-time problem.

blocks.subTitle: Functional
blocks.markdown:
What the system must do:

- **Request a ride** — a rider gives a pickup and drop location; the system finds a driver.
- **Match the nearest available driver** to the request.
- **Trip lifecycle** — a trip moves from requested to assigned, started, and completed (or cancelled).
- **Fare estimate** — quote a price up front, including **surge pricing** when demand is high.
- **Ratings** — rider and driver rate each other after the trip ends.

blocks.subTitle: Non-functional
blocks.markdown:
What the system must guarantee, not just do:

- **No double-assignment** — a driver must never be matched to two trips at once, even with concurrent requests.
- **Low-latency matching** — nearest-driver search must stay fast as the number of drivers grows into the millions.
- **Consistency of driver state** — location and availability must reflect reality, not a stale cache, or matching sends riders to drivers who already left.
- **Extensibility** — new matching heuristics or pricing rules should slot in without rewriting the trip engine.

**Noun extraction** turns requirements into candidate classes; verbs that don't belong on a data object become strategies or state behavior instead.

| Noun in requirements | Becomes |
|---|---|
| rider, driver | `Rider`, `Driver` (both extend a `User` base) |
| trip, fare, rating | `Trip`, `Fare`, `Rating` |
| location, pickup, drop | `Location` (geo coordinate) |

"Matches the nearest driver" and "computes a fare" are policies, not fields — they become `DriverMatchingStrategy` and `PricingStrategy`. "Moves through states" becomes `TripState`, a **State** pattern rather than a status enum with branching `if` chains.

- **State** replaces a `status` field and scattered `if` checks — each state class knows only its own valid transitions.
- **Strategy** interfaces sit outside the `Trip`/`TripService` hierarchy so matching and pricing evolve independently of each other and of the trip itself.

blocks.subTitle: Location, Rider & Driver
blocks.markdown:
`Location` is a plain geo point reused everywhere distance matters. `Driver` carries live location and an availability flag that matching reads on every request.

```text
class Location:
    latitude: float
    longitude: float

    method distanceTo(other: Location): float:
        return haversineDistance(this, other)   // great-circle distance

abstract class User:
    id: String
    name: String
    rating: float = 5.0

class Rider extends User:
    paymentMethod: PaymentMethod

enum DriverStatus:
    AVAILABLE
    ON_TRIP
    OFFLINE

class Driver extends User:
    vehicle: Vehicle
    location: Location
    status: DriverStatus = OFFLINE

    method updateLocation(loc: Location):
        this.location = loc                 // pushed by driver app every few seconds

    method isAvailable(): boolean:
        return status == DriverStatus.AVAILABLE
```

blocks.subTitle: TripState — the State pattern
blocks.markdown:
Each state is its own class holding only the transitions valid from that point — a driver can't "complete" a trip that was never started, and the compiler-level structure enforces it instead of an `if` chain.

```text
interface TripState:
    method assignDriver(trip: Trip, driver: Driver)
    method start(trip: Trip)
    method complete(trip: Trip)
    method cancel(trip: Trip)
    // default: throw InvalidTransitionException() for anything not overridden

class RequestedState implements TripState:
    method assignDriver(trip, driver):
        trip.driver = driver
        driver.status = DriverStatus.ON_TRIP
        trip.state = new AssignedState()
    method cancel(trip):
        trip.state = new CancelledState()

class AssignedState implements TripState:
    method start(trip):
        trip.startTime = now()
        trip.state = new StartedState()
    method cancel(trip):
        trip.driver.status = DriverStatus.AVAILABLE
        trip.state = new CancelledState()

class StartedState implements TripState:
    method complete(trip):
        trip.endTime = now()
        trip.fare = trip.pricingStrategy.calculateFare(trip)
        trip.driver.status = DriverStatus.AVAILABLE
        trip.state = new CompletedState()

class CompletedState implements TripState:
    pass   // terminal — no overrides, every action throws

class CancelledState implements TripState:
    pass   // terminal
```

blocks.subTitle: Trip
blocks.markdown:
`Trip` holds the data; it delegates every transition to its current `TripState` instead of checking a status field itself.

```text
class Trip:
    id: String
    rider: Rider
    driver: Driver = null
    pickup: Location
    drop: Location
    state: TripState = new RequestedState()
    pricingStrategy: PricingStrategy
    fare: Money = null
    startTime: DateTime = null
    endTime: DateTime = null

    method assignDriver(driver: Driver):
        state.assignDriver(this, driver)

    method start():
        state.start(this)

    method complete():
        state.complete(this)

    method cancel():
        state.cancel(this)
```

blocks.subTitle: DriverMatchingStrategy — the matching problem
PricingStrategy — fare and surge
blocks.markdown:
Fare rules change constantly — base rates, surge multipliers, promos — so pricing stays out of `Trip` entirely.

```text
interface PricingStrategy:
    method calculateFare(trip: Trip): Money

class BasePricingStrategy implements PricingStrategy:
    baseFare = 2.50
    perKm = 1.20
    perMinute = 0.20

    method calculateFare(trip): Money:
        distanceKm = trip.pickup.distanceTo(trip.drop)
        minutes = minutesBetween(trip.startTime, trip.endTime)
        return Money(baseFare + distanceKm * perKm + minutes * perMinute)

class SurgePricingStrategy implements PricingStrategy:
    private base: PricingStrategy
    private demandService: DemandService

    constructor(base, demandService):
        this.base = base
        this.demandService = demandService

    method calculateFare(trip): Money:
        multiplier = demandService.currentSurgeMultiplier(trip.pickup)  // e.g. 1.0-3.0
        return base.calculateFare(trip) * multiplier
```

blocks.subTitle: TripService — the coordinator
blocks.markdown:
`TripService` is the entry point riders and drivers actually call — it wires the strategies to the trip without containing the matching or pricing logic itself.

```text
class TripService:
    private drivers: List<Driver>
    private matchingStrategy: DriverMatchingStrategy
    private pricingStrategy: PricingStrategy
    private locationObservers: List<LocationObserver>

    method requestTrip(rider: Rider, pickup: Location, drop: Location): Trip:
        trip = new Trip(rider, pickup, drop, pricingStrategy)
        driver = matchingStrategy.findDriver(pickup, drivers)
        if driver == null:
            throw NoDriverAvailableException()
        trip.assignDriver(driver)            // atomic claim, see Concurrency card
        notifyObservers(trip)
        return trip

    method startTrip(trip: Trip):
        trip.start()

    method completeTrip(trip: Trip):
        trip.complete()
        rateParticipants(trip)

    method estimateFare(pickup: Location, drop: Location): Money:
        return pricingStrategy.previewFare(pickup, drop)
```

Where each pattern earns its place in this design:

| Pattern | Where it's used |
|---|---|
| State | `TripState` — Requested/Assigned/Started/Completed/Cancelled with legal transitions only |
| Strategy | `DriverMatchingStrategy` (nearest/ETA) and `PricingStrategy` (base/surge) |
| Observer | Driver location updates and rider notifications pushed to subscribers |

Each replaces logic that would otherwise sit inside `TripService` as branching conditionals. See [behavioral-patterns-i](behavioral-patterns-i) for the general form of State and Strategy, and [behavioral-patterns-ii](behavioral-patterns-ii) for Observer.

blocks.subTitle: Observer for location and notifications
blocks.markdown:
A driver's location update and a trip's state change both have multiple interested parties — the rider's map, the ETA service, an analytics pipeline — none of which the source object should know about by name.

- `Driver.updateLocation()` and `TripService.notifyObservers()` publish an event; each `LocationObserver` or `TripObserver` subscribes independently.
- Adding a new listener (e.g. fraud detection watching sudden location jumps) never touches `Driver` or `TripService`.
- This is the same decoupling idea covered in [concurrency-in-oo-design](concurrency-in-oo-design) — producers and consumers of state shouldn't be wired together directly.

blocks.subTitle: Two riders, one driver
blocks.markdown:
**The classic bug**: two riders request a ride at nearly the same instant, both matching queries see the same driver as the nearest available one, and both trips get assigned to them.

- The race is **check-then-act**: "is this driver available" and "assign this driver" are two separate steps unless made atomic.
- Fix: guard the claim with a per-driver lock, or a **compare-and-swap** update — `UPDATE drivers SET status = 'ON_TRIP' WHERE id = ? AND status = 'AVAILABLE'` — and check the affected row count. Zero rows means someone else won the race; fall back to the next candidate.
- At Uber's scale this claim happens in a dispatch service backed by a fast key-value store, not an in-process lock, since matching runs across many machines. See [concurrency-in-oo-design](concurrency-in-oo-design).

How the design absorbs real follow-up requirements without a rewrite:

- **Pooled rides** — add a `PooledTrip` that holds multiple riders and stops; `TripState` transitions stay the same shape, only the data on `Trip` grows.
- **Scheduled rides** — add a `ScheduledState` before `Requested` that waits until pickup time, then hands off to the existing flow untouched.
- **Trade-off**: `TripState` as full classes is more ceremony than a status enum for a small system — worth it here because trip transitions are exactly the kind of rule that changes and needs enforcing, not everywhere.

blocks.subTitle: Matching a rider to the nearest driver
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: How do you match a rider to the nearest driver at scale?**

A linear scan over every driver, as in the pseudocode, doesn't survive millions of drivers. Real systems index drivers into a spatial structure — a **geohash** grid or **quadtree** — bucketed by area, so a request only scans drivers in nearby cells. `DriverMatchingStrategy` is the seam: swap `NearestDriverStrategy`'s naive scan for a geohash-backed lookup without touching `TripService`.

blocks.subTitle: Modeling the trip lifecycle
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: How do you model the trip lifecycle so invalid transitions are impossible?**

Use the **State** pattern: each state (`RequestedState`, `AssignedState`, `StartedState`, `CompletedState`, `CancelledState`) implements only the transitions legal from that point, and everything else throws by default. This beats a `status` string with `if state == "assigned"` scattered across the codebase — the compiler-visible interface, not a comment, tells you what's allowed next.

blocks.subTitle: How surge pricing fits in
blocks.markdown:
**Q: How does surge pricing fit into the design without complicating Trip?**

`SurgePricingStrategy` wraps a `BasePricingStrategy` and multiplies its result by a demand-based factor from a `DemandService` — a **decorator-flavored Strategy**. `Trip` and `TripService` only ever call `pricingStrategy.calculateFare(trip)`; they never know whether surge is active. Swapping pricing logic never touches trip or matching code.

blocks.subTitle: Avoiding double-assignment
blocks.markdown:
**Q: How do you avoid assigning one driver to two riders at once?**

Make the read-and-claim a single atomic step, not a separate check then update. Use a conditional update (`WHERE status = 'AVAILABLE'`) or a distributed lock keyed on the driver ID, and check whether the claim actually succeeded. If it didn't, another request won — fall back to the next-nearest candidate instead of failing the rider outright.

blocks.subTitle: Which patterns fit and why
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Which design patterns fit ride-hailing, and why?**

State for the trip lifecycle, since transitions must be restricted and the rules are exactly the kind that grow over time (pooled rides, scheduled rides). Strategy for matching and pricing, since both are policies that change independently of the trip and of each other. Observer for location and notification fan-out, since many consumers need the same event without being coupled to the source.
